newsitem.title: UK: Freight rates soar, spectacular rebound seen.
newsitem.headline: Freight rates soar, spectacular rebound seen.

text.p: Bigger demand than was expected for grain and minerals in Asia's booming economies has caused a spectacular recovery in world freight rates, after they had collapsed only a few weeks ago to the lowest in a decade.
The cost of seaborne freight is up 50 percent in two months mainly on demand for ships to take grain, coal, ores and fertiliser to Asia. Higher oil prices also put up bunker costs.
Firmer rates delight owners even as the volatility baffles charterers.
"People who felt the market was weak suddenly found that they had to scratch around to cover requirements," said John Banaszkiewicz at brokerage CIS in London.
One barometer is the Baltic Freight Index (BFI), a daily index of rates on key dry cargo routes which is compiled by London's Baltic Exchange, a hub of international chartering.
The BFI registered a huge fall from a historic peak of 2,352 points in May 1995 to a low at 992 this September.
It was ending this week almost at 1,500. Friday saw the biggest single day's gain for 18 months, up 44 points to 1,477.
Shipbrokers blamed the decline earlier this year on a glut of new ships entering the market for bulk dry cargo -- grains, coal and ores. Tankers form a separate market.
It also looked as if bumper harvests in Australia and China would keep freight rates under pressure.
These signalled that Asia might need less grain and that more of what was required would be supplied on short haul intra-Asian routes rather than from the Americas.

But at the height of the grains season the Chinese this year suddenly seemed to be shopping for more American soybeans than had been expected. Mineral and fertiliser demand in Asia was also unexpectedly strong.
Take the case of Silver Star, a vessel of 69,235 deadweight tonnes in the Panamax class.
London brokers say they heard it was fixed earlier this week for three to five months at $10,500 a day. Then it was re-let at $10,900. And by week's end it had been re-let again for $11,500.
"We usually see an upswing in the fourth quarter but there has been a psychological shock this year," said Banaszkiewicz at CIS.
"How much longer can it go on? We should see a correction at some point but it might be postponed until after Christmas. Fundamentals for the end of the year and for 1997 do not look that good."

He and other analysts argue that new tonnage continues to leave shipyards. One vessel of the big Capesize class and two in the smaller Panamax category of up to 75,000 deadweight tonnes have been entering the market each week.
